articles.title: Thailand bank offers employees aged 45-59 up to a year's salary to retire early amid AI shift; CEO says scheme cuts costs; Kasikornbank steps up automation to boost productivity
articles.summary: As Thailand struggles with slow economic growth, Kasikornbank CEO Kattiya Indaravijaya is preparing the country's third-largest bank for a
articles.body: As Thailand struggles with slow economic growth, Kasikornbank CEO Kattiya Indaravijaya is preparing the country's third-largest bank for a technology-driven future. Her plans include a voluntary early retirement scheme for employees aged 45 to 59, greater use of artificial intelligence (AI) and a push to expand businesses beyond traditional lending.Called "45 is the new 60", the programme offers eligible employees standard retirement compensation and additional severance of up to a year's salary. It is part of a wider effort to reduce costs and improve productivity as Thailand's economy loses pace.Over the past five years, Thailand's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by an average of 2.34% annually, behind regional neighbours such as Malaysia and Vietnam, which recovered more quickly after the pandemic. Kattiya believes the country needs to rethink the industries that once drove its growth."We need to restructure our economy, [because] the growth engines back then are not the growth engines now," she told Fortune.The same approach applies to the bank. "Because the economy is like this, we cannot just think about revenue generation," she said. "[We have to consider] cost savings too, so we're working on a lot of productivity improvements."'45 is the new 60': early retirement as technology changes jobsKasikornbank introduced the voluntary retirement scheme last year. Employees aged 45 to 59 can apply to leave with their standard retirement compensation and additional severance of up to 12 months' salary.Kattiya said the offer is intended partly for staff who are uncomfortable with the pace of technological change or do not feel able to reskill for new roles."Those who know that technology is coming in and feel that they are unable to reskill, or feel uncomfortable, they can take this package out," she said.Many employees took up the offer, she added, helping bring down personnel expenses this year. The initiative comes as banks increasingly use automation and AI to handle routine tasks, changing the skills required across the industry.Thailand needs to move beyond assembly-line manufacturingKattiya argues that Thailand must develop new sources of growth rather than rely on sectors that no longer offer the same competitive advantage. She pointed to electronics manufacturing, where rising labour costs are putting pressure on the country's position.In her view, Thailand needs to move beyond assembling products and build expertise in designing and manufacturing higher-value goods."Instead of just assembling things, we should innovate and create things of value," she said.She wants Thailand to use investments by advanced electronics companies to build local capabilities. Negotiations with incoming firms should include knowledge-sharing and opportunities for local businesses to learn how to manufacture more sophisticated products."That's how knowledge transfer can happen," she said.From Thai Farmers Bank to a leading lenderFounded in June 1945 as Thai Farmers Bank, Kasikornbank initially provided financial services to farmers, who made up a large part of Thailand's population. It adopted its current name in 2003 as manufacturing and services became more important to the country's economy.The bank ranked No. 37 on Fortune's Southeast Asia 500 list. In 2024, it recorded a profit of 49.6 billion Thai baht, or about $1.5 billion, the highest among local banks, according to Thai newspaper The Nation.Kattiya joined the bank in 1987 as a relationship manager in its manufacturing and agriculture lending department. She recalled that Kasikornbank was already known for introducing new ideas, including becoming Thailand's first bank to offer credit card services in 1973.She later held six roles across business development, corporate strategy and executive services. She became president in 2016 and CEO in 2020, the first woman in the bank's history to hold both positions. She is ranked No. 33 on Fortune's Most Powerful Women in Asia list.'3+1' strategy targets growth beyond loansKattiya faced pressure to improve the bank's performance after the pandemic slump. During her first roadshow as CEO in 2023, she met shareholders in Hong Kong, Singapore, London, New York and Boston. Investors wanted stronger profitability, double-digit return on equity and better shareholder returns."They weren't quite happy," she said. "They expected stronger profitability, double-digit return on equity (ROE), and better total shareholder returns."In response, she introduced the "3+1" strategy. Its three priorities were to reinvigorate credit, expand fee income and offer customers banking services across digital and physical channels. The additional focus was investment in innovation to create new revenue streams.The bank has since worked to reduce its reliance on interest income from loans by expanding wealth management and payments. It is also exploring regional expansion and partnerships. In 2025, Kattiya updated the strategy to "3+1&P", adding productivity as another priority, with technology and AI central to the plan.AI tools aim to give staff more time with customersOne of the first AI projects under the productivity push is an AI-enabled operating manual for employees in call centres and branches. Kasikornbank has hundreds of products and handles a wide range of customer situations. The tool can search thousands of pages of instructions and tell staff what customers should expect and which documents they need."We have hundreds of products, and hundreds of events that can happen," Kattiya said. "The AI will read through thousands of pages in the operating manual, and tell them what exactly to tell customers to expect and which documents to bring. This gives employees more time to interact with our customers."The aim is to reduce time spent searching for information and allow employees to focus on customer service.KBTG builds the bank's technology capabilitiesKasikornbank established the Kasikorn Business-Technology Group (KBTG) in 2016 as a separate entity to accelerate innovation and manage its digital infrastructure. Its roughly 2,000 employees work in a separate building with a more informal, technology-company culture, including casual dress, nap pods, an ice-cream corner and an amphitheatre."For banks, we have to dress in suits to gain the trust of customers," Kattiya said. "But we felt that [the engineers] should be in a different environment... If we want them to be innovative, their working environment should be out of the box as well."KBTG developed the K PLUS mobile banking app, launched in October 2018. It lets users pay bills, transfer money and manage their finances. The app now has more than 24 million users and around 30% of Thailand's digital payment and mobile banking market share.In 2024, KBTG launched AINU, an AI-powered digital identity verification platform that is also offered to smaller banks as an electronic know-your-customer solution.CEO wants to learn before adopting every new AI toolDespite its investments, Kasikornbank is taking a measured approach to AI. Kattiya said the bank does not need to be among the first to adopt every new technology and can learn from global companies that move faster."Even our board wants us to be on the first wave, but I feel like we don't really need to be on the first wave on every technology," she said.She cited companies such as Google as technology leaders whose experience can help banks assess and implement new tools."It's smarter to learn from global technology leaders [like Google] who move fast and move first… then they can help us implement what they learn," she said.Kasikornbank is monitoring developments and testing AI on a smaller scale before making wider commitments. Kattiya said the bank wants to ensure its systems are ready before moving ahead."We'll stay close and keep learning," she said. "We want to make sure that the tracks are ready before we get on the high speed train."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI has finally given gamers something they have spent years waiting for, and some of the internet’s biggest streamers wasted no time diving into the action. Adin Ross, Kai Cenat, IShowSpeed and xQc were among the early players to explore Rockstar Games’ latest release. Their first streams quickly turned into viral moments, with unexpected character interactions, police chases and bizarre in-game discoveries giving fans an early taste of what makes GTA VI so different.IShowSpeed, Kai Cenat and Adin Ross discover GTA VI’s wildest momentsThe first wave of GTA VI livestreams offered plenty of entertainment beyond the usual gameplay. IShowSpeed, known for his unpredictable reactions, quickly found himself exploring some of the game's more unusual character interactions.One moment that caught viewers' attention involved protagonist Jason taking a shower while Lucia joined him. Speed could barely keep his excitement to himself as he sang, “Don’t stop the rain, girl,” during the scene. The unexpected interaction became one of the early talking points from his stream.Kai Cenat also had an eventful start. During his first mission, a glitch appeared to disrupt the expected sequence of events. An animation bug allowed him to escape the police, even though the mission was reportedly designed to end with his character getting arrested. The moment quickly circulated online, giving fans another reason to discuss the game's unpredictable behaviour.Adin Ross took a different approach to exploring Vice City. His gameplay included attacking non-playable characters and police officers to collect money. However, his actions soon attracted unwanted attention. The game's wanted system kicked in, giving him a three-star wanted level and triggering a police chase.Meanwhile, xQc spent much of his early gameplay enjoying the quieter details. Rather than constantly chasing action, he watched television inside the game and had Jason work on renovating his home.GTA VI surprises players with celebrity references and unusual encountersThe excitement surrounding GTA VI extends beyond its gameplay mechanics. Rockstar has packed the fictional world with cultural references, familiar music and unexpected details that have already sparked conversations online.One particularly unusual feature involves a fictional radio exchange between far-right personalities Nick Fuentes and Alex Jones. Jones appeared to enjoy the reference, posting, “I like it a lot…” Fuentes, however, seemed less certain about the portrayal."People are saying this is me and Alex Jones… Is that supposed to be me? Doesn't really sound like me,” he reportedly said during a livestream, according to Newsweek.Music is another major attraction. Miami rapper JT, formerly of City Girls, appears as a radio host, while the game's soundtrack includes artists such as Cardi B, Travis Scott, Rauw Alejandro and Zara Larsson.Players have also spotted a dog riding a jet ski to Jagged Edge's 2001 hit "Where The Party At." articles.title: Trump, Xi agree on need for AI safety rules, US-China cooperation on regulations
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he and Chinese President Xi Jinping agree on the need for regulations to ensure artificial intelligence (AI) is
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has said he and Chinese President Xi Jinping agree on the need for regulations to ensure artificial intelligence (AI) is developed safely, adding that the two countries will work together on what he described as reasonable rules.In an interview with Fox News on Thursday, Trump said both leaders wanted safeguards for the rapidly advancing technology, as the United States and China compete to develop more powerful AI models.Trump also said he did not discuss Nvidia or its CEO Jensen Huang's alleged links to a Chinese spy in detail during his meeting with Xi in Shenzhen earlier this week.The Chinese embassy in Washington echoed the call for cooperation, saying the two countries should "strengthen communication and coordination, prevent the security risks of AI and ensure that AI is always under human control."The comments come as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in artificial intelligence, a technology both countries consider strategically important for military capabilities and technological dominance.Nvidia, the world's leading maker of advanced chips used to develop cutting-edge AI models, sits at the centre of this rivalry. The US has sought to restrict China's access to Nvidia's most powerful chips over concerns that they could strengthen the Chinese military.Trump's remarks on Huang came amid a report by The New York Times in October that the Nvidia chief had a romantic relationship with a woman accused of spying for Beijing.Asked about the issue, Trump said he had not spoken much with Xi about Nvidia or Huang's relationship with the woman during their discussions.Meanwhile, Trump said after talks with Xi Putin that a mutual pact to limit nuclear weapons will be hard to achieve but that he will keep working on it. "I love the concept of it but in terms of pure negotiation, it’s a very hard thing for me as a president to do," Trump told Reuters.Trump, Xi meet in Shenzhen amid wider geopolitical tensionsTrump met Xi in Shenzhen this week as part of a series of high-level engagements on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The two leaders discussed issues including trade, Iran and the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, according to reports.Trump also took part in a trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. The roughly 70-minute meeting focused on nuclear risks, among other issues, but produced a limited set of areas for cooperation.The three leaders expressed interest in reducing nuclear dangers and reforming the United Nations. Trump described the meeting as "Highly Consequential", while Xi called it positive, constructive and fruitful, according to the Associated Press.The Shenzhen engagements come amid tensions over the wars in Ukraine and Iran, as well as the broader contest between Washington and Beijing over technology, trade and military influence.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jogar lixo na rua pode render multa de mais de R$ 3,2 mil em Goiânia | G1
articles.standfirst: Projeto de lei também prevê recompensa a ser paga a quem denunciar descarte irregular à prefeitura. Proposta foi aprovada em primeira discussão pela Câmara Municipal.
articles.summary: Projeto de lei também prevê recompensa a ser paga a quem denunciar descarte irregular à prefeitura. Proposta foi aprovada em primeira discussão pela Câmara Municipal.
articles.body:
Um projeto de lei que prevê o pagamento de multa de até R$ 3,2 mil para quem jogar lixo na rua foi aprovado em primeira discussão pela Câmara Municipal de Goiânia . Atualmente, quem comete a infração na capital pode ser multado entre R$ 6 e R$ 132.

A proposta de aumento do valor inclui outra mudança: a possibilidade de multa ser aplicada também para empresas e entidades, e não a apenas pessoas físicas, como é hoje.

De acordo com o texto do projeto de lei, as penalidades passarão a ter os seguintes valores:

Infrações leves : 1/3 do salário mínimo vigente;

Infrações médias : metade do salário mínimo vigente;

Infrações graves : 1 salário mínimo vigente;

Infrações gravíssimas : 2 salários mínimos.

Uma regulamentação específica vai definir os critérios para a classificação das infrações. No entanto, segundo apuração da TV Anhanguera, as multas mais pesadas serão aplicadas, por exemplo, em casos de descarte em áreas mais sensíveis, como de proteção ambiental permanente e próximo a nascentes.

Descarte irregular de lixo em Goiânia pode render multa de até 2 salários mínimos — Foto: Reprodução/TV Anhanguera

Se aprovada, a nova legislação prevê, ainda, uma recompensa de 20% do valor arrecadado com a multa para quem fizer a denúncia sobre o descarte irregular à gestão municipal.

No caso de reincidência do infrator, o valor da multa aumenta em até 50% na primeira reincidência e até 100% na segunda.

De acordo com a proposta, a arrecadação com as multas será revertida para diversos fins:

Manutenção, recuperação e instalação de lixeiras públicas e outros equipamentos de limpeza urbana;

Execução de serviços de limpeza e remoção de resíduos lançados irregularmente em vias públicas;

Realização de campanhas de educação ambiental e conscientização sobre o descarte correto de resíduos.

O projeto de lei, de autoria do prefeito Sandro Mabel (União), ainda precisa ser aprovado em segunda discussão pelos vereadores e, depois, ir à sanção.

articles.title: Motociclista morre em batida frontal no contorno da Rodovia dos Tamoios, em Caraguatatuba  | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente ocorreu na noite da última quinta-feira (19).
articles.summary: Acidente ocorreu na noite da última quinta-feira (19).
articles.body:
Motociclista morre em batida frontal no contorno da Rodovia dos Tamoios — Foto: Divulgação/Artesp

Um motociclista morreu na noite da última quinta-feira (19) após uma batida frontal contra um carro que fazia uma ultrapassagem pela contramão no contorno da Rodovia dos Tamoios, no km 6, em Caraguatatuba .

De acordo com a concessionária que administra a rodovia, as cinco pessoas que estavam no carro saíram ilesas. Ainda não há informações sobre o que ocorreu com o motorista do carro e dados da vítima.

O acidente ocorreu por volta das 21h30. A concessionária informou que o carro trafegava pela pista sentido leste e, ao fazer uma ultrapassagem pela contramão, invadiu a pista do sentido oposto e bateu de frente com a moto.

A vítima foi removida pela funerária às 23h40. Houve interdição total da pista sentido leste e oeste por um período. A liberação total ocorreu no início da madrugada desta sexta-feira.

articles.title: Trump backs firing of US cyber chief Sean Cairncross amid tech outages
articles.summary: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is set to leave his post amid a spate of technology disruptions affecting critical infrastructure,
articles.body: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is set to leave his post amid a spate of technology disruptions affecting critical infrastructure, financial institutions and government networks across the country. Kirsten Davies, currently the chief information officer at the Department of Defense, is expected to take over in an acting capacity. Axios was first to report the personnel changes.A person close to the White House told news agency AFP on Thursday that Cairncross had been "fired" from the position. The source also said that US president Donald Trump "fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position", citing concerns that he lacked the appropriate credentials for the role.However, a separate account cited by Fox News suggested that Cairncross did not wish to serve another two years in the position. His departure date remains unclear.According to NBC News, Davies, who currently serves as the Defence Department's Chief Information Officer, will take over temporarily. The source said she had more appropriate credentials and had been confirmed by the US Senate.The National Cyber Director's position requires Senate confirmation, making the appointment of a permanent successor a separate process. Cairncross has headed the Office of the National Cyber Director since August 2025. The office is responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government.Before taking up the position, Cairncross held several roles in the White House during Trump's first administration. He also served as the Republican National Committee's Chief Operating Officer during the 2016 election cycle. Cairncross declined to comment on his departure.The personnel change comes after a series of disruptions affecting major American technology and public services. These included a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop, an outage affecting Microsoft's Outlook email services, disruptions involving United Airlines and major banks, and a temporary interruption to an internal National Security Agency (NSA) communications network.The developments have prompted questions about the resilience of critical infrastructure and the administration's handling of the incidents. However, the country's top intelligence official said on Wednesday that the disruptions were separate service outages linked to maintenance and technical changes, rather than evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored cyberattack.Financial institutions have also reported security concerns. JPMorgan Chase disclosed on Thursday that third-party service providers working with the bank had been targeted in a cyberattack. According to reports, information potentially exposed included customer names, email addresses, phone numbers and account identifiers. The bank said its investigation indicated that attackers accessed certain marketing data held by vendors.Trump, meanwhile, sought to play down public concerns over the disruptions. Speaking to Fox News ahead of the APEC Summit, he said, "Tell them to relax. Everything's good. These are individual events. So, Chase Manhattan Bank, JPMorgan, it goes out. Somebody else goes out. And I also think that, the press is sort of having a lot of fun with it."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: At least six people, including a child, were killed after a suspected gas explosion caused part of a five-storey residential building to collapse in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, on Thursday.The explosion occurred on Thursday morning in the suburban Ponichala district, leaving several residents buried beneath the rubble.Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili said rescue teams had recovered six bodies, including that of a young child, Al Jazeera reported.A three-year-old girl was rescued alive after being trapped under the debris for several hours.Emergency Management Service chief Teimuraz Mgebrishvili said one of the women found dead was believed to be the girl's mother, according to AFP.The girl was taken to Ingorokva University Clinic, where doctors said she was in stable condition and scans had found no serious traumatic injuries, Georgian Public Broadcaster (1TV) reported. An 11-year-old boy was also receiving treatment in intensive care, with his condition described as relatively stable.Tamazashvili said preliminary findings suggested that the blast originated on the building's fifth floor when a resident tried to switch on a gas heater.However, gas supplier Tbilisi Energy said the apartment suspected to be the source of the explosion was registered as unoccupied and had recorded no gas consumption over the past year, according to 1TV. The company added that it had not yet been able to inspect the damaged property.Following structural assessments, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said 28 families, comprising more than 100 residents, would be temporarily moved to hotels because two sections of the building had been declared unsafe, Al Jazeera reported, citing Georgia's Interpressnews agency.Prosecutor Levan Vepkhvadze said authorities had opened a criminal investigation into possible violations of safety regulations.You use AI every day. articles.title: A van Gogh with a complex past sells for a record $190 million at auction
articles.summary: LONDON: A vibrant landscape painted by Vincent van Gogh weeks before his death has sold for $190.4 million at auction, a record for a work by the artist.
articles.body: LONDON: A vibrant landscape painted by Vincent van Gogh weeks before his death has sold for $190.4 million at auction, a record for a work by the artist."Chataigniers en fleurs" (Chestnut Trees in Flower) exceeded its $180 million estimate at a Sotheby's auction in New York on Wednesday. The sale went ahead after an agreement between its current owners and the heirs of a Jewish family that sold it in Nazi-era Germany.A day before the auction, Sotheby's announced an agreement between the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which has owned the painting since 1975, and the descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, who sold it in 1936.A lawyer for the Fischer heirs had asked for the sale to be postponed until Sotheby's showed the painting had not been sold under duress.The auction house said that "in recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution." It did not disclose details of the agreement.The Fischer heirs said they were "grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby's and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era."Van Gogh painted "Chataigniers en fleurs" in a burst of creativity after his release from a psychiatric asylum in May 1890. He took his own life two months later.The previous record for a van Gogh was $117.2 million paid for "Verger avec cypres" (Orchard with Cypresses) at a Christie's auction in 2022.Paul Cezanne's portrait "Arlequin" sold for $111 million in Wednesday's sale of a dozen Impressionist and post-Impressionist works amassed by the late Argentine art collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her sugar magnate husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier.The 12 works sold for a total of $412 million.You use AI every day. articles.title: Drinking 2 to 3 cups of caffeinated coffee a day was linked to far lower dementia rates in US adults followed for up to 43 years, 141 versus 330 cases per 100,000 a year, while decaf showed no such link
articles.summary: A cup of good coffee is probably the first thing that our hand reaches for every morning, but do you know that your daily cup of coffee might be doing
articles.body: A cup of good coffee is probably the first thing that our hand reaches for every morning, but do you know that your daily cup of coffee might be doing more for you than you realise? And no, it's not bad news. While most of us associate coffee with staying awake, fighting morning sluggishness or getting through a particularly exhausting day, for many, it’s a small cup of joy, with people waiting for the entire day just for the feeling of that first sip of coffee. But now, researchers have found another possible reason to keep that cup within reach.A long-term study involving more than 130 thousand US adults has found that people who regularly drank caffeinated coffee had considerably lower rates of dementia than those who consumed little or none. Interestingly, the association was not observed among people who preferred decaffeinated coffee. Those who consumed around two to three cups of caffeinated coffee a day showed the strongest association with lower dementia risk, raising fresh questions about the role caffeine and other coffee compounds may play in long-term brain health.The research, titled “Coffee and Tea Intake, Dementia Risk, and Cognitive Function”, was published in the journal JAMA and analysed data from two long-running US health studies, the Nurses' Health Study and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study. It included 131,821 participants, comprising 86,606 women and 45,215 men, whose dietary habits and health outcomes were tracked not over a few months or years but over several decades. Researchers collected information through questionnaires conducted every two to four years, examining participants' consumption of caffeinated coffee, decaffeinated coffee and tea, alongside their overall caffeine intake.What did the 43-year study actually find?After following the participants for several decades, researchers began noticing an interesting pattern. Those who regularly consumed caffeinated coffee appeared to have a considerably lower rate of dementia than those who drank very little or none.For those who don’t know, according to the Alzheimer’s Association, dementia is a general term for conditions that progressively interfere with the brain’s cognitive functioning, including memory, thinking, language, mood and behaviour.Out of the 131,821 participants, 11,033 developed dementia during the follow-up period. When researchers compared people with the highest and lowest caffeinated coffee consumption, the difference was quite striking. The former recorded 141 cases per 100,000 person-years, while the latter recorded 330.But the findings became even more interesting when researchers looked at how much coffee people were drinking. The strongest association with a lower dementia risk was observed among those consuming around two to three cups of caffeinated coffee every day. However, drinking more did not necessarily mean better results, suggesting that the relationship between coffee consumption and brain health may not be as straightforward as simply having another cup.How much coffee is enough to see a difference?The study found that the association was strongest among people who drank around 2–3 cups of caffeinated coffee a day. Interestingly, drinking more coffee did not appear to offer additional benefits, suggesting that higher consumption does not necessarily mean a lower risk of dementia. Researchers also found a similar association among people who consumed around 1–2 cups of tea daily, with the strongest association observed at approximately 300 mg of caffeine a day.However, not all coffee showed similar results. While caffeinated coffee consumption was associated with lower dementia rates, researchers did not find a statistically significant association among people who drank decaffeinated coffee.Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee, tea and other plants. It is the compound that gives you the sensation of being energised and reduces feelings of tiredness. This difference raises questions about whether caffeine itself, or perhaps other compounds found alongside it in caffeinated coffee, could be involved in the observed association.The difference between regular and decaffeinated coffee makes this possibility worth investigating; however, the study did not establish caffeine as the cause of the observed benefits.For now, the findings offer an interesting insight into the relationship between everyday dietary habits and long-term brain health, but they are not a reason to start drinking coffee solely to prevent dementia. Since the research was observational, it cannot establish that caffeine directly reduces the risk of developing the condition. The participants were also largely healthcare professionals, so further research involving more diverse populations will be needed to understand whether the same association holds more widely. Until then, the study adds another piece to the growing conversation about how lifestyle and diet may be linked to cognitive healthYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Maximise probability of success, accept uncertainty
articles.summary: By Dhruva Bhargava The universe is built on a paradox: uncertainty is the only certainty.
articles.body: By Dhruva BhargavaThe universe is built on a paradox: uncertainty is the only certainty. While modern science continues to peel back layers of reality, a complete understanding of existence remains elusive. The deeper we explore, the more mysterious the cosmos becomes. Upanishads anticipated this cosmic enigma, describing a reality that is simultaneously hidden and self-revealing, veiled by a cosmic illusion.This profound mystery is beautifully captured in Isha Upanishad, which describes the supreme reality as a mind-bending paradox: it is static yet dynamic, local yet infinite, hidden deep within atoms while entirely enveloping the cosmos. Investigating this reality through external observation alone is impossible. Kena Upanishad explains that our sensory instruments – eyes, words, and thoughts – are inherently limited. What we perceive as absolute reality is merely a deception of the senses. Colours do not exist objectively; they are our brains’ translation of a tiny band of the electromagnetic spectrum. Sound does not exist in a vacuum; it is merely our ears interpreting air-pressure waves. This aligns with the Mandukya Upanishad, which asserts that the outer world does not exist independently of observer, but rather mirrors our internal awareness.At the fundamental level, the material universe lacks solidity and certainty we attribute to it. The illusion of a smooth, continuous world shattered when Max Planck discovered quanta, proving that radiation is emitted in discrete packets. Our brains only perceive continuity because these packets are released with immense intensity. Furthermore, atoms are not solid spheres. If a nucleus were the size of a football in the centre of a stadium, the nearest electron would sit at the farthest stand, leaving the atom 99.9% empty space. Even nuclear decay highlights this cosmic randomness; while we know Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5,730 years, predicting exactly which atom will decay next remains impossible.This fundamental unpredictability extends to the passage of time. The laws of thermodynamics state that entropy constantly increases, endorsing change as an inescapable property of nature. Similarly, the Katha Upanishad defines the material world as anitya, impermanent, warning that relying on transient material fruits yields only temporary solace, making anxiety inevitable for those who cling to them. In such a universe, scientific inquiry can only improve our predictive probability. We can measure humidity, temperature, and atmospheric pressure, yet predicting actual rainfall remains probabilistic. A flawless driver, fully confident in their safety, can still be involved in an unexpected accident.The human implications of this perpetual flux are immense. Because failures, setbacks, and mishaps are inevitable, navigating life is a constant challenge. Humans naturally respond to unpredictability with anxiety, fear, and helplessness. However, the wisdom of Gita clarifies that it is not the external situation, but our response to it, that dictates our suffering. Krishn reminds us that what we possess today belonged to someone else yesterday and will change hands again tomorrow. By attaching ourselves to the impermanent, we invite sorrow. We interact with this uncertain universe through karm – our intentions and actions – but the ultimate outcomes are governed by variables far beyond our control. Gita does not deny cause and effect; instead, it emphasises that total control over results is an illusion. We have agency only over our efforts and inner virtues, such as courage, patience, and perseverance. By focusing on continuous, noble effort, we maximise our probability of success while gracefully accepting the inherent uncertainty of existence.Disclaimer: Views expressed above are the author's own.

articles.title: 'Everybody's got an opinion': Rahul Gandhi explains why he is called a youth leader at 56
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi responded to being called a 'youth leader' despite being 56, saying age should not define youth.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi responded to being called a 'youth leader' despite being 56, saying age should not define youth. In a conversation, Rahul said remaining curious and never being afraid to ask questions, even those considered unusual or ridiculous, was what kept a person young.During a conversation at the University of Chicago, Rahul said he had never accepted the idea that certain questions should not be asked and believed curiosity across subjects was what defined youth."Look, everybody's got an opinion, okay? So somebody will say, I'm a youth leader. Somebody will say, I'm an old people's leader. Somebody will say something else. I mean, it's fine. Everybody is allowed to have a perspective," Rahul said.Responding to a question about why young people identify with him, Rahul Gandhi said he had been encouraged from an early age to remain curious and ask questions across different subjects."But I was taught when I was small to always be curious and to not have boundaries on your curiosity. So to ask questions in all spheres, you know, ask a question about geopolitics, ask a question about women's health, ask a question about animals, ask a question about pretty much anything," he said.He added that society gradually places restrictions on people's curiosity as they grow older, encouraging them to focus on conventional measures of success."So what society is going to try and tell you as you progress is that there are certain questions you can't ask, and there's certain questions that you just shouldn't ask. And there is a set of questions that you can ask," Rahul Gandhi said."You know, you can ask, how do I make money? You can ask, how do I own a big house? You can ask, how do I do well at work as adults? But then there's a whole bunch of questions you're not allowed to ask. I never bought into that."He cited the example of his former mathematics tutor, whom he met for breakfast and learnt was pursuing a master's degree in his 60s.Rahul Gandhi said people should continue asking questions, including those that others might consider unusual or uncomfortable."And to me, that is what you have right now that you should never lose, never be scared of asking the most ridiculous questions, questions that people just will not ask themselves. And that's what youth is. So maybe that's why they say I'm a youth leader," he said.The conversation also turned to generational change in political leadership, particularly in the United States, where younger leaders from different political camps are emerging.Asked about the youth movement in American politics, Rahul Gandhi said he had noticed a shift in how Western leaders approached international affairs. He recalled that leaders he encountered early in his political career had a broader understanding of global developments."I noticed something in leadership in the West. Right. And I noticed when I first came into politics, the leaders had a pretty good understanding of. Of the rest of the world. There was a decent sense. I remember having a conversation with Mr. Tony Blair, and I was like, okay, he gets Afghanistan or he has a sense of India," he said.However, Gandhi said he later encountered leaders who appeared more focused on domestic issues and had limited understanding of developments in other countries."And then suddenly in the middle, I found a group of leaders who were focused completely on what was going on in their country. And they would come, and I'm not saying one particular country, they'd come. And it was obvious that they didn't have the grounding or understanding of our stuff," he said.Rahul Gandhi also referred to Russian President Vladimir Putin while discussing leaders with a broader understanding of geopolitics."At risk of getting into trouble. Mr. Putin has one of the most profound geopolitical minds that I have come across. He can talk in massive sweep about these type of things. And I think that was the thing that. That struck me. There was a moving inwards of Western leadership," he said.He added that Western leaders had increasingly focused on domestic issues rather than developments beyond their borders."you know, looking inside and focusing on the home more than outside. That's just an experience I had. I don't know if I'm correct or wrong," Congress leader said.He also suggested that some younger leaders were beginning to show a wider interest in international affairs."But the reason I said that is that some of these young guys, they seem to be re looking at the outside world. They seem to be having now a vision of a bigger scope than earlier," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Address: Tihar Jail, work: To Kill': How D-Company-linked gangster Naseem Durrani's long run ended in UP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: For years, Naseem Durrani moved between the gritty turf wars of northeast Delhi and the far-reaching shadow of Mumbai’s underworld — a man
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For years, Naseem Durrani moved between the gritty turf wars of northeast Delhi and the far-reaching shadow of Mumbai’s underworld — a man whose criminal ledger stretched from neighborhood extortion rackets to alleged hit contracts tied to Dawood Ibrahim’s "D-Company."Beyond his crimes on the ground, Naseem actively used social media to cultivate a climate of fear among people. His Instagram profile served as an overt display of intimidation, featuring a bio that read: "Name: Badnaam (Notorious) | Address: Tihar Jail | Age: To live | Work: To kill." Through this digital persona, he openly advertised his criminal background while remaining absconding from law enforcement.On Friday, that long run ended in a hail of gunfire in Uttar Pradesh’s Bulandshahr district, where a joint operation by the Noida Special Task Force (STF) and Delhi Police cornered and killed the wanted gangster.How the net closed inActing on intelligence inputs tracking Durrani’s movements, Delhi crime branch team led by DCP Sanjeev Yadav and deputy superintendent of police R K Mishra from STF Noida mounted a coordinated operation in Bulandshahr, supervised by special CP HGS Dhaliwal.In the early hours, the cops detected his movement near the Sikandra Bypass. CCTV footage showed him riding a scooter, and when the police team moved in to arrest him, he repeatedly looked back at the pursuing officers while speeding away.​During the chase, Naseem's scooter skidded and fell. Armed with two .32-bore pistols, he opened fire on the police team, prompting officers to retaliate. He sustained multiple gunshot wounds in the exchange of fire, and police recovered both pistols from the spot.A chequered historyThe breakthrough came days after a brazen daylight-style shooting in northeast Delhi put law enforcement on high alert. Investigators had been scanning CCTV footage, tracing escape routes, and following leads in the wake of a deadly attack in Khajuri Khas.While police files linked Durrani to more than 25 criminal cases — spanning murder, attempt to murder, and robbery — his profile extended well beyond local street crime. The first was a killing outside Delhi law minister Kapil Mishra's camp office where 26-year-old Sameer was shot dead with over a dozen rounds fired in the attack.Police scrutiny following the recent violence has pointed to a prolonged gang feud in northeast Delhi, allegedly driven by extortion demands targeting shared auto-rickshaw operators and scrap dealers. Durrani had also previously been named as a key accused in the May 26 killing of Raja Mewati, alias "Akki Don," in Khajuri Khas.Investigators noted that Durrani had links to Dawood Ibrahim’s D-Company and remained in contact with underworld figure Chhota Shakeel. According to reports, Shakeel had allegedly handed Durrani a contract during 2016–2017 to eliminate rival gangster Chhota Rajan, who was lodged in Tihar Jail.With Durrani killed in the Bulandshahr encounter, investigators are expected to examine how his network operated across the Delhi-NCR and western Uttar Pradesh belt, as well as any lingering fallout from the ongoing turf wars in northeast Delhi.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Thousands protest Colombia’s tax plans amid row over US military role
articles.summary: Trade unions, students and opposition groups demonstrated in Bogota and other major cities on Thursday.
articles.body:
Thousands of Colombians have taken to the streets in a second nationwide protest against President Abelardo de la Espriella, opposing proposed tax reforms and rising living costs as his government faces scrutiny over plans for closer military cooperation with the United States.

Trade unions, students and opposition groups demonstrated in Bogota and other major cities on Thursday against proposals to lower the income tax threshold, increase healthcare contributions and reduce corporate taxes.

“A large part of Colombia feels vulnerable. The rich are the ones who are getting more money,” Leidy Gutierrez, a 21-year-old psychology student, told the AFP news agency.

The proposed reforms would require Colombians earning more than about $985 a month to pay income tax, down from the current threshold of about $1,419.

De la Espriella’s government says the measures are necessary to raise revenue amid a fiscal crisis, with next year’s deficit projected to reach 9.4 percent of gross domestic product. The president has already withdrawn a controversial proposal to raise taxes on basic food products following widespread criticism.

Former President Gustavo Petro, who has backed the demonstrations, urged Colombians to mobilise against policies he said threatened household incomes.

De la Espriella said citizens were free to demonstrate peacefully but warned that he would not tolerate road blockades or what he described as “urban terrorism”.

The marches were mostly peaceful, but some ended in clashes with riot police, who fired tear gas and water cannon, AFP reported.

The demonstrations came as the president and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected a New York Times report claiming Bogota had turned down a proposal for joint US-Colombian military operations against drug trafficking groups on Colombian territory.

The newspaper reported on Wednesday, citing US officials, that de la Espriella had told Washington he lacked sufficient support in Congress to authorise the operations, prompting Hegseth to shorten his visit to Colombia.

A US official told the Reuters news agency that concerns existed in Bogota over congressional support but did not confirm that the Colombian president had rejected the proposal outright.

De la Espriella denied rejecting any proposal from US President Donald Trump’s administration, saying cooperation with Washington was aimed at strengthening Colombia’s military capabilities rather than seeking the deployment of American troops. He stressed that any such deployment would require congressional approval.

During his visit to Bogota on Wednesday, Hegseth praised Colombia’s participation in the US-led Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, an initiative aimed at strengthening regional military cooperation against organised crime.

The protests were the second nationwide mobilisation since de la Espriella took office in August. Tens of thousands demonstrated in October against what opposition groups described as an erosion of human rights and social reforms introduced under Petro.

articles.title: ‘We don’t want our future decided by the military’: Young Germans protest
articles.summary: Ahead of Friday’s nationwide rallies, German teenagers explain why they are resisting conscription.
articles.body:
Berlin, Germany – Last month, high school student Phil Werring received a letter from the German Armed Forces, known as the Bundeswehr.

In an official document, a military registration form, Werring was asked to answer compulsory questions – and optional ones if he was interested in joining the army.

After initially ignoring the first letter, two weeks later he received another, warning him of a 250 euro ($275) fine if he did not answer.

Logging in via a QR code, he started working his way through the questionnaire.

“The mandatory questions included ones on whether you have any diseases, your weight, height and whether you played sports, while other questions asked about whether you had a driving licence and what languages you spoke,” the 18-year-old, who lives with his three younger siblings and parents in Muenster, western Germany, told Al Jazeera.

“I only answered the mandatory questions, so it took me around 15 minutes to complete, but if I had filled it all out, it would have taken me a lot longer. I know that not answering all the questions can increase my chances of being called in by the military for a check-up, but I still didn’t want to answer them all.”

Official figures show that by the end of October, nearly 600,000 letters had been sent out this year to young Germans, of which about 286,800 were sent to young men and 271,700 to women and people of other genders. The form is only mandatory for men to complete.

Military conscription, meanwhile, has been a headline-grabbing issue in Germany since the start of the year, after the Military Service Modernisation Act came into effect on January 1 . It set out new targets to grow the army by the mid-2030s, increasing its full-time force to about 260,000, plus 200,000 reservists.

The recruitment drive is one element of Germany’s broader military expansion plans, initiated in 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Berlin is also increasing defence budgets and surveillance powers for intelligence services.

According to the Ministry of Defence, its efforts are yielding positive results. Official figures indicate that the Bundeswehr has already exceeded the statutory force build-up range for 2026, with personnel numbers in October about 6,400 higher than the same month last year.

Yet as recent protests have shown – including a series of school strikes and a large-scale demonstration organised by a loose alliance called “Gen Z Regelt” (Gen Z Sorts It) – many young people are pushing back against the plans.

Gen Z Regelt is rallying again on Friday, with nearly 20,000 people across 40 cities, including Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich, signed up so far.

“The military questionnaire had many personal questions, and I found the experience quite scary, and it made me angry,” Werring said. “As I filled out the form, I realised how serious the government is about taking these steps to reintroduce compulsory military service, and that I may have no choice but to serve and risk my life for companies making millions selling arms. It made me realise that I must be active against these steps towards militarisation and support resistance efforts against these war preparations.”

‘Students worry about the roof falling on them’

Linus Schneider, 16, fears that as more money goes towards rearming Germany, the less there is for schools like those in his home city of Munich, which are not in good shape.

“The roofs have been leaking at my school for three years now,” he told Al Jazeera. “Something wasn’t installed properly when the building was built a few years ago, and the city has been saying that they don’t have as much money as they did a few years ago, so they can’t fix the issue. This has led to a lot of problems at school; for example, sometimes we can’t have gym class at all because there are buckets of water in the sports hall.”

Munich is the largest city in one of Germany’s wealthiest states, Bavaria.

Schneider added, “I also hear from friends in other schools that their roofs are in such a bad condition that they are worried about the roof falling on them. We literally don’t have good roofs over our heads. There are big cuts to education and healthcare, while at the same time, military spending has increased drastically.”

According to the current draft budget for 2027, to be agreed on later this month, defence spending is expected to rise to 109.7 billion euros ($120.5bn) from 82.7 billion euros ($90.8bn) the year before. The Ministry for Education and Family, meanwhile, projects a budget of 15.9 billion euros ($17.5bn) compared to 16.6 billion euros ($18.3bn) this year.

Sebastian Koos, a sociologist at the University of Konstanz who researches youth and protest movements, said the wave in Europe was an “important spark” for the German movement.

“There are some similarities and overlaps with the problems, such as the cost of living and cuts to education. But I think the issue of military conscription makes the situation for young people here unique,” he told Al Jazeera.

Koos said that while several different organisations participate in the Gen Z Regelt protests, a common thread is a sense of hopelessness.

“There are also many issues and demands that are being put together. They are also worried about economic and social inequality, right-wing extremism, the cost of living, as well as climate change. This is a lot to digest, and it is very difficult to get a sense of hope if you are confronted with so many different conflicts.”

Friday’s protest will include thousands of students protesting against compulsory military service, organised by the youth-led alliance, School Strike Against Conscription.

Werring will be among those taking to the streets in his local area.

“I’m still figuring out what I want to study, but I am interested in the medical sector. I want to help people, not shoot or harm anyone. I don’t want my future to be interrupted by the military,” he said.

Schneider is in trouble with the school head teacher for getting involved in the protests, but he still plans to join Friday’s rallies.

“We want to make our own decisions about our future,” he said. “We don’t want our future to be decided by the military or the state. And I think that’s quite an important reason why we’re protesting. We also didn’t want war. I think it’s crucial that we stand together in the face of these increasing state repression that [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz is overseeing.”

articles.title: EU-UK talks: New deal should reduce 'Irish Sea border' impact
articles.summary: The agreement is expected to be confirmed when Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen meet in Brussels.
articles.body:
A new deal between the UK and the EU on food, plants and animals is likely to be significant for Northern Ireland by reducing the impact of the "Irish Sea border".

The agreement is expected to be confirmed later when Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels.

Since Brexit, Northern Ireland has continued to follow EU rules for agri-food products while the rest of the UK has not.

The new deal will see the whole UK realigning with EU rules on those products, meaning goods being sent from Great Britain to Northern Ireland will no longer need to be checked at ports.

It will also mean a reduction but not elimination of the paperwork required to move agri-food goods from Great Britain to Northern Ireland.

The Irish Sea border refers to checks and controls on goods entering Northern Ireland from the rest of the UK.

It came about as the result of a Brexit deal between the EU and UK in 2019. The deal was revised in 2023 and is now known as the Windsor Framework.

It was agreed that the most practical way to keep the border open between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland after Brexit was for Northern Ireland to follow EU laws on the regulation of goods.

However that means that goods coming from the rest of the UK into Northern Ireland face paperwork and other restrictions to ensure they meet EU standards.

Food products and plants face the most bureaucracy and this continues to cause problems for retailers .

For many nationalists in Northern Ireland, this has been a necessary compromise to minimise the impact of Brexit on the island of Ireland.

For many unionists it is a constitutional affront which undermines Northern Ireland's place in the UK.

The largest unionist party, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), prevented Northern Ireland's power-sharing government from operating between 2022 and 2024 in protest at the sea border.

Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said what has been suggested so far "seems to be positive" in terms of further collaboration and removal of "some of the barriers that had been erected by Brexit".

"I think what it actually points to is what an unmitigated disaster Brexit has actually been," she told Good Morning Ulster.

"It has been an act of economic self-harm for Britain and particularly from an economic perspective."

Archibald said in terms of the deal, she thinks "it's positive, it's moving in the right direction".

"Anything that reduces friction for our businesses in terms of trade is a positive thing in that regard," she added.

"And then there are some other elements of the deal like in respect of youth mobility that are positive also."

How would an agri-food deal change things?

Switzerland's borders with the EU illustrate what will change.

Like the UK Switzerland is not a member of the EU but there are no regulatory border controls for trade in agri-food products between Switzerland and the EU.

That is because the Swiss agreed to follow EU rules almost to the letter, without much say in setting those rules.

Switzerland is obliged to modify its laws in response to changes in EU legislation, what is known as dynamic alignment, and accept oversight from the European Court of Justice.

It is a Swiss-style deal which the UK and EU are now on the verge of finalising.

Such a deal would mean the sea-border controls on Great Britain food products entering Northern Ireland could be effectively ended.

Border control posts built at Northern Ireland ports would become largely redundant, although pre-Brexit checks on livestock would continue.

The "Not for EU" labels seen on Great Britain food products sold in Northern Ireland would no longer be needed.

One deals with products' standards - making sure goods can be legally sold.

The other deals with customs - making sure the correct tariffs have been paid.

An agri-food deal would go a long way to removing the standards border but it would leave the customs border untouched.

Businesses in Great Britain would still have to make customs declarations for goods going to Northern Ireland with the risk that goods would be delayed if the paperwork is incorrect.

Meanwhile unionist parties have issued a joint statement criticising the UK government for refusing to block an update to the EU customs rules which apply in Northern Ireland.

On Tuesday, Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant declined to use the blocking mechanism known as the Stormont Brake .

The statement, from the DUP, the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) and Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV), said the "new iteration of the customs border" would deny Northern Ireland "unfettered access to critical inputs and finished goods from the greater part of its home market

The BBC understands that a deal on electricity, which could cut costs for Northern Ireland consumers, will not be part of this agreement.

There had been speculation that a "recoupling" of the EU and UK electricity grids would form part of the package.

Northern Ireland's energy regulator has said such a move could reduce wholesale electricity prices in Northern Ireland by up to 20%.

An electricity deal remains under negotiation and could still be agreed at a later date.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We will not provide a running commentary on ongoing discussions.

"We are negotiating a deal to link our electricity market with the EU that will cut bills for both households and businesses, and strengthen our energy security."

articles.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
articles.summary: Would AI be a good judge of whether you should get a mortgage, car loan or mobile phone contract?
articles.body:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.

Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.

"I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls.

"When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies."

That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.

Their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.

The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.

Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".

"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics."

Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".

As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.

"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there."

Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.

Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.

"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.

"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," says Olufunwa.

articles.title: Thomas Markle ruled mentally competent to face trial
articles.summary: A judge in Florida on Thursday declared Thomas ​Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, to be mentally competent to answer to a federal court charge accusing him of being ‌a child sexual predator.
articles.body: TAMPA, Florida — A U.S. judge in Florida on Thursday declared Thomas ​Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, to be mentally competent to answer to a federal court charge accusing him of being ‌a child sexual predator. Accepting the findings of a court-appointed forensic psychiatrist, U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin ruled the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry was mentally fit to understand the proceedings against him and to properly assist in his own defense, court records showed. Neither prosecutors nor the defense disputed the findings of the psychiatrist’s evaluation, contained in a 15-page report and based in large part on the doctor’s in-person interview ​with Markle in prison last week. Markle was charged November 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images. According to an FBI ​affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question, including two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and ⁠other images of him with children in various stages of undress, was found in two Los Angeles storage units. Commenting on the case at the time of Markle’s arrest on November ​6 at an assisted-living center in Florida, FBI Director Kash Patel said Markle had “targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions.” Griffin’s ruling capped a competency proceeding set in ​motion by the judge after Markle’s first court hearing on the day of his arrest. In ordering a psychiatric examination of the defendant, Griffin wrote that she found “reasonable cause” to believe Markle was suffering from some mental deficiency, based in part on his advanced age and “lack of recall” during his first court appearance the day of his arrest. Dr. Aime Gerodimos, who conducted the evaluation, wrote in her report that Markle ​appeared to suffer from a “major neurocognitive disorder,” possibly the result of mild vascular disease. She also found he was likely “exaggerating deficits” when asked to recall specifics of the allegations ​against him. The psychiatrist concluded that Markle “does have sufficient present ability to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him and to assist properly in his defense” — the legal standard for ‌a criminal ⁠defendant to be deemed competent. Case originated in Philippines Markle was first taken into custody at the assisted-living facility where he was residing in Lakeland, Florida, near Tampa. Griffin initially ordered him placed under home confinement on condition that Markle wear an electronic monitoring device. But days later, the judge revoked the arrangement and ordered him back to jail without bond after Markle cut off his electronic ankle tag with a knife. It remained unclear when Markle would be transferred to federal custody in California, where the case against him was lodged. The judge on Thursday set a preliminary hearing ​in the case for December 1 in ​Tampa. According to the FBI affidavit, federal agents acting ⁠on a search warrant earlier this month seized a large cache of slides, film negatives and books from two storage lockers Markle had rented in Los Angeles since 2008. One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appears to be part of ​a motel chain in the Philippines, where Markle previously resided and where authorities initiated an investigation of him last month, the ​affidavit said. Philippine police said on Wednesday ⁠criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country’s Cebu province, where he lived. The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police said. Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as “sick lies.” Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the ⁠run-up to her ​marriage to King Charles’ younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became ​aware of the allegations against her father. She has said she was “deeply distressed” over the matter, which led her to cut off contact between her father and her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

articles.title: The young star painter seducing the art world with glittering curtains. (Just don’t ask what’s behind them)
articles.summary: Louise Giovanelli has become a bright spot in the art world for her ominous, radiant drapes. Ahead of her new exhibition in London, she refuses to pull them back.
articles.body: “Curtains make people behave very differently,” said Louise Giovanelli. The young British painter has seen it first-hand. Her life-size oil paintings of undulating drapes, where folds of velvet or tinsel absorb and refract the glow of a stage spotlight, often become the backdrop for art gallery selfies. “People always go and take selfies in front of the curtains,” she said. “They don’t do it in front of any other painting.” This partition of fabric, Giovanelli thinks, gives people “permission” to perform. Karaoke, theater, even bingo night — “it’s a signal for people,” she said, sitting in a tidy upstairs meeting room at the White Cube gallery in central London. Curtains are not classist, either. “You see them in very grand theatrical contexts, like theaters and cinemas and The Proms,” she said of the prestigious British classical music festival. “But then you also find them in seedy nightclubs and brothels and working men’s clubs.” In the last five years, the 33-year-old has become an art world bright spot for her ominous, radiant drapes painted Old Masters-style with slow, painstaking brushwork. Glitter curtains, she said, are the hardest for their layers of pointillist work: “It’s like a constellation of stars, you get lost in the image trying to find the star that you just put in.” Giovanelli had her first solo exhibition right out of art school, where low studio rent in her adoptive home of Manchester meant she could survive as a working artist immediately. She first caught the attention of critics and gallerists in a 2021 survey of contemporary painting at The Hayward Gallery in London. “She’s one of the most skilled painters I know,” said Marie-Charlotte Carrier, a curator at the Hepworth Wakefield gallery in the north of England, who sought Giovanelli out after coming across her work at the group show. “She’s so knowledgeable about art history, techniques, pigments and oils. She thinks about every single layer of paint she puts on her work.” Then came a flurry of exhibitions — including one commissioned by Carrier — in Yorkshire, Blackpool, London, Manchester (where Giovanelli is still based), and internationally in New York, Munich, Amsterdam, China and next year, Paris. She typically works across 10 to 15 paintings at once, starting one while waiting for another to dry — a method that means she has a prolific output, though she hazards a guess that each canvas takes around two months to complete. Last fall, she dolled-up an 18th century church in the middle of the capital with a giant painted silver shimmer curtain, her first public art installation. Her ascent has been dubbed meteoric by some — does she feel it? “I don’t know,” she said. “When you’re in it, you never really feel it do you?” Below us, busy hands work to set up her latest show, “In the Light of False Suns,” in time for opening night. Walls are re-painted white, on which one of Giovanelli’s holographic “wig paintings,” as she calls them, leans while it waits to be hung. Titled “Media Luna,” it marks Giovanelli’s newest accolade: being named recipient of the Robson Orr TenTen prize last month. Cascading locks of hair dominate the image, brushed so smooth disco light pools on the lacquered strands. Fifteen prints were commissioned for the British government’s permanent art collection –– which also holds two Giovanelli paintings –– and will be displayed in British government buildings and embassies around the world. Hair is another key motif for Giovanelli. “If they’re shown next to curtain paintings, they become curtains,” she said. “Like veils or draperies.” Curtains, hair, even a hanging meat carcass — a new experimental subject matter for Giovanelli brought on by a recent trip to an abattoir — are all gilded by her brush. “I’m interested in the dazzle, the glitz, the glamour because it’s kind of a modern form of worship. We don’t go to church anymore,” she said, but “we still have this human need to point at something, to worship something, someone.” Giovanelli herself grew up in Wales in a home of Sunday church-goers. As a child, her Italian father and Irish mother were both practicing Catholics. She was drawn to the ornate altars, the icons rendered in stained glass, but most of all the luminescence of religious imagery. At art school in Manchester and Germany, she became consumed by Renaissance and pre-Renaissance painting — even when her peers were swept up by post-modernist cynicism. “I was just in the corner every hour of the day painting these like Old Master rip offs,” she said. “I was perceived to be very uncool by doing that.” Today her work hinges on the assumption that, whether its 1606 or 2026, we are all still like moths to a flame. “That’s why I called it ‘In the Light of False Suns,’” she said of the show. “I’m just thinking of all the different forms of light: light emanating from the canvas, light coming from a source that’s depicted in the picture.” But instead of the Virgin Mary, Giovanelli is often painting Sissy Spacek, Christina Ricci, Chloë Sevigny — the devotional icons of our time. “I’m always trying to bridge these historical understandings with a more contemporary vision,” she said. Some of her canvases are cut to be long and thin, mimicking “totems,” columns or phone screens. But “collectors love paintings that go that way,” she motions horizontally. “Because they go above people’s sofas.” Giovanelli doesn’t know much about the sofas her paintings hang above these days. As a fresh graduate she sold her work directly, now that’s handled by the gallery. Once upon a time an established art institution told Giovanelli she would struggle to get any collectors at all, given she is based in the north of the country. “Things are definitely changing,” she said. “I think people are realizing that most art is not made in London.” She has helped re-shape that thinking, in part with Apollo School — a free, not-for-profit painting program she co-founded in 2023 with curator Alice Amati and Dr. Ian Hartshorne, former head of painting at Manchester School of Art. Together, they take on a cohort of five students for an intensive course of practical painting technique and guest lecturers with insider industry knowledge, like how to decipher the legalities of consignment agreements. “I saw it advertised on Instagram,” said current student and oil painter Grace McNerney, who applied because “I knew who Louise was, because every painter around now does.” McNerney said she learnt basic skills like how to prime a canvas, how to use mediums, and things that she found had fallen off conventional bachelors programs focused on multi-disciplinary teaching. “There was a real emphasis on cutting the shit and looking at young artists and saying, ‘We’re going to teach you about things like color theory,’” she said of Apollo School. “We think we can offer in three months far more than what most art schools offer in three years,” said Giovanelli. Downstairs, two new works both titled “Ad Astra” are the gravitational center of the exhibition. They each show the same scene, an erotic open-mouthed woman illuminated onto a huge run of iridescent curtains, at different crops. (“Cropping is very important for me because you’re cropping out information that would otherwise give away the full story”). It’s the first time Giovanelli has combined two of her artistic obsessions on top of each other. The glowing ethereal face is one she has painted many times before, inspired by a scene in the 1971 French horror film “Don’t Deliver Us from Evil,” where Catholic schoolgirls are receiving the Eucharist. “It felt like each image was charging each other,” she said. “But what’s also important in these works is that the curtain still remains completely closed,” she said. “Which is something I get asked all the time. ‘What’s behind the curtain?’” she imitates. “You’re asking the wrong question.”
