articles.title: Medicare for All sounds free. But wait until you see your huge tax bill
articles.summary: Medicare for All could end health insurance premiums and deductibles, but a CBO-modeled plan might add $3 trillion in federal spending annually by 2030.
articles.body: Imagine a politician knocking on your front door with the greatest financial offer in American history. No more health insurance premiums. No more deductibles. No more copayments. And everybody gets healthcare courtesy of Uncle Sam. Sounds fantastic, doesn't it? EL-SAYED ADMITS FREE HEALTHCARE MEANS PAYING 'A LITTLE BIT MORE IN TAXES' REGARDLESS OF INCOME There's just one tiny problem. Your doctor isn't working for free. Your hospital isn't operating for free. And the government doesn't have a magical money tree growing behind the White House. Welcome to Medicare for All, where the healthcare might be free at the doctor's office, but the bill eventually shows up somewhere else. Usually in your paycheck. DSA LEADER DISMISSES $49T COST ESTIMATE FOR SOCIALIST POLICIES AS A 'MADE-UP NUMBER' The $30 trillion elephant in the room Let's start with some numbers. LET SOCIALISTS ROB FROM THE RICH 100% AND YOU STILL WON’T BE ABLE TO PAY THE BILLS The Congressional Budget Office has modeled single-payer healthcare systems that would increase federal healthcare spending by approximately $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion annually by 2030. That's potentially $30 trillion over a decade at the upper end of that annual range. For perspective, America's entire federal government collected roughly $5.4 trillion in revenue in fiscal 2026. $50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT Think about that. We're talking about adding a massive new federal financing responsibility to a government already carrying more than $40 trillion in debt. HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY' Supporters correctly point out that Americans would no longer pay many private insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs. But eliminating your insurance premium doesn't eliminate the underlying medical bill. It just changes who sends you the invoice. Congratulations! Your premium is now a tax THE DSA’S DANGEROUS FINE PRINT. THEY'RE COMING FOR MILLIONAIRES (AND YOU) The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget examined what financing approximately $30 trillion in additional federal spending over 10 years might require. The Congressional Budget Office has modeled single-payer healthcare systems that would increase federal healthcare spending by approximately $1.5 trillion to $3 trillion annually by 2030. One illustrative option was a 32% payroll tax. Another was a 25% income surtax. DEPROGRAMMED: A 'KIND OFFER' OF DEATH SENT THIS COUPLE RUNNING FROM UNIVERSAL HEALTH CARE Those aren't official Medicare for All proposals. They're examples of the scale of taxation potentially required if either tax were used alone. And here's where the political sales pitch gets interesting. A family might save thousands in premiums and deductibles but pay substantially more in taxes. Another family could come out ahead. The result depends on income, healthcare needs and the financing structure. You can't determine whether Medicare for All saves your family money until somebody tells you exactly how they're paying for it. Your insurance card doesn't create another doctor Here's another inconvenient detail. If millions more Americans can obtain medical services without worrying about bills, demand for care could increase. That's potentially good for people who currently go without treatment. But who's providing all those additional appointments? We already have shortages of healthcare professionals in many communities. Expanding coverage without expanding medical capacity can create longer waits for some services. And if Washington attempts to control spending by reducing reimbursements, hospitals and physicians face another challenge. You can promise everybody a doctor's appointment. You can't legislate another 100,000 doctors into existence overnight. What happens to the insurance you already have? Nearly half of Americans are expected to receive employer-sponsored health coverage in 2026. A comprehensive Medicare for All proposal would fundamentally replace that system. Some Americans would welcome the change. Others might lose coverage arrangements, provider networks or benefits they currently prefer. Employers would face major adjustments, too. We're talking about adding a massive new federal financing responsibility to a government already carrying more than $40 trillion in debt. And don't forget that Medicare itself isn't free today. Beneficiaries commonly pay Part B premiums, face deductibles and often purchase supplemental coverage. A proposed Medicare for All system with no premiums or deductibles would actually be more generous in important respects than traditional Medicare. That generosity comes with a price tag. The government can't repeal economics Here's what bothers me most about the Medicare for All debate. Politicians talk about healthcare as though the primary challenge is deciding who deserves coverage. The harder financial question is how America delivers affordable, high-quality care without bankrupting families, overwhelming taxpayers or destabilizing hospitals. The United States spent approximately $5.3 trillion on healthcare in 2024. We absolutely need to address prices, administrative waste, prescription drug costs and access to medical care. A single-payer system might reduce some of those expenses. But the savings aren't guaranteed, and neither is a painless transition. The real question isn't whether Americans deserve healthcare. Of course, they do. It's whether Washington can finance and administer an enormously expanded system without creating a different set of financial problems. When a politician tells you something costing trillions of dollars will be free, don't ask where to sign up. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ask where they're hiding the bill. articles.title: Youth-led strikes sweep Europe as students protest rising cost of living and war
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of young people are slated to fill Europe’s streets on Friday – in an organized international youth-led day of action across more than 25 nations.
articles.body: Tens of thousands of young people are slated to fill Europe’s streets on Friday – in an organized international youth-led day of action across more than 25 nations. Student groups in the UK, France, Spain, Italy and beyond will walk out over the sky-rocketing cost of living, rising tuition fees, underfunded education systems and what they cast as leaders’ complicity in Israel’s war in Gaza. Earlier this fall, Gen-Z protests erupted over growing disenchantment that governments have not future-proofed against unregulated artificial intelligence, high unemployment and the climate crisis. Up to 10,000 students are expected to participate in rallies in Germany’s western city of Cologne, CNN affiliate RTL Germany reported. Thousands of people have started to march in cities across Italy, according to CNN affiliate Sky TG24, with students in Rome, Genoa, Bologna and Milan calling for an end to rearmament. In Britain alone, students from more than 350 schools, colleges and universities will walk out, according to Socialist Students, one of the groups taking part. “Young people will not sit quietly while our schools, colleges and universities are cut and billions are found for war,” the national chair of Socialist Students, Adam Powell-Davies, said in a statement. “Fight for our future, not their wars.” In Italy’s capital, Rome, protesters chanted and held up an array of slogans including “Money for schools, not war,” and “We want to live life without the high cost of living,” according to Sky TG24.

articles.title: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.summary: Deals on food and animal goods, mobility and student fees have been agreed, but months of negotiations lay ahead.
articles.body:
The European Union has struck agreements on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.

After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.

“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.

Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.

A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.

“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”

Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.

The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.

The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.

The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.

Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.

Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.

However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.

That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.

Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.

The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

articles.title: Deadly Russian strikes hit 3 Kyiv bridges after Putin vows revenge for Crimea attacks
articles.summary: Three bridges in Kyiv were hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, officials in the Ukrainian capital said, after President Vladimir Putin vowed revenge.
articles.body: KYIV, Ukraine — Three bridges in Kyiv were hit in a massive Russian ballistic missile attack, officials in the Ukrainian capital said Friday, hours after President Vladimir Putin vowed “painful” revenge for strikes on his prized bridge linking Crimea to Russia. The attacks, which started in the early hours of the morning and continued well into the day damaged the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges connecting the left and right banks of the Dnipro River, which flows through the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a post on Telegram. At least six people were killed and 15 injured in the strikes on the capital, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a separate post. Two others were killed in separate attacks across the country, which saw nine regions hit overnight, he said. The strikes on Kyiv forced authorities to restrict traffic on the bridges, impacting the movement across the capital, and Klitschko asked residents not to drive private cars into the city “unless absolutely necessary” and suggested employers should let staff work remotely. Russia has been hitting Kyiv’s Southern and Northern bridges since early October, causing multiple closures, disrupting metro services and causing traffic jams — complicating day-to-day life in the city that’s home to millions of people. But it is the first time that Russia hit three different bridges in a single night, and it has left most of the main road crossings over the Dnipro damaged or restricted at the same time. An NBC News team in Kyiv heard air raid sirens going off every few minutes overnight, accompanied by loud explosions. After dawn broke on the rainy and foggy Friday morning, firefighters were seen putting out the flames from a strike on an industrial area in the capital. It’s part of the daily reality for Kyiv’s residents after Russia escalated both the number of ballistic missiles it was firing at the capital and the frequency of attacks. The latest strikes came hours after Putin said that Moscow would hit back hard after Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week. Speaking in the Chinese city of Shenzhen after his much-touted trilateral meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Putin said Moscow would hit back hard for the attacks on his flagship project. The Kerch Bridge was meant to solidify Russian dominance over Crimea, the peninsula he illegally annexed in 2014. “We will respond to these strikes. I want everyone to know that,” Putin told reporters, adding that Russia’s response will be “far more painful” than what Kyiv did to the Kerch Bridge, which cost billions of dollars to build. Putin personally opened the road and rail bridge, which is the longest in Europe, in 2018. Beyond its symbolic value, the bridge has served as a vital supply route for the Russian military and civilians in Crimea to cross onto the Russian mainland and back. Putin insisted Thursday that the bridge was “an exclusively civilian facility,” but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called it “the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea.” On Friday, Zelenskyy said that Russia’s attempts to justify its attacks as “responses” to any of his country’s own attacks should be unacceptable. “Putting Russia and Ukraine on an equal footing is fundamentally wrong,” he said, adding: “This week, Putin posed for photographs with world leaders. But the photograph he deserves is one of him in the dock, where he stands trial for crimes against Ukrainians and Ukraine.” Acknowledging the strikes on Kyiv’s bridges Friday, Russia said they were used for military purposes — the line of reasoning Moscow has used in the past to justify bridge attacks in Kyiv. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s air force said Friday that Russia used ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as more than 400 drones, in the massive attack against 23 locations across the country. The country’s energy authorities also said Russian strikes on power plants and substations, which have been ongoing since early fall, left people in Kyiv and 10 other regions without power. Richard Engel and Michael Fiorentino reported from Kyiv. Yuliya Talmazan reported from London.

articles.title: The collapse of Trump’s blood diesel scheme is a victory for Ukraine
articles.summary: The war still hangs in the balance, but the failure of Trump and Putin to break the sanctions regime is a victory for Ukraine in its gallant fight for survival.
articles.body:
President Trump triumphantly announced last month that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin had struck a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel. Tankers carrying diesel departed from Russia’s Baltic Sea port of Primorsk, bound for ports on the U.S. East coast.

Some tankers veered away to South America. One steamed into the Mediterranean, and another zig-zagged aimlessly in the Atlantic. They were looking for buyers elsewhere in the world, because U.S. diesel importers, port managers and terminal operators, did not want anything to do with Russia’s “blood diesel.”

It is blood diesel the way “blood diamonds” have financed wars in West Africa. Proceeds from the deal between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin would have helped to finance Putin’s war machine, which has killed or injured tens of thousands of Ukrainian civilians, including 3,000 children, and displaced millions.

The diesel-laden tankers were modern-day blockade runners, trying to evade U.S. and international sanctions against Russia. But the U.S. companies, under pressure from outraged senior Democrats and Republicans in Congress who claimed that the deal was illegal, passed on the diesel. They feared both reputational damage and legal jeopardy for violating the sanctions regime.

The diesel deal was in part a political stunt, so that Trump could tell midterm voters that “ lower prices for Americans is my Greatest Priority.” But the small quantity of diesel involved would have had no appreciable impact on soaring U.S. diesel prices, and voters certainly didn’t seem impressed by the deal.

In the context of Trump’s history of appeasing Putin and pushing Ukraine to make unilateral concessions, it was also a means for Trump to further pressure Ukraine into capitulation by degrading the sanctions regime. Zelensky has candidly acknowledged that “we will not prevail ” if the U.S. sides with Russia, which appears to be Trump’s ambition. He has signaled that he is willing to accept most of the Kremlin’s demands to achieve peace. But a peace on Putin’s terms, which will exclude a European security force to defend Ukraine, will inevitably lead to full Russian occupation and the end of Ukrainian statehood.

In the parts of Ukraine they have already occupied, Russian forces have detained, tortured and executed Ukrainian military officers, cultural figures and political leaders down to the village level , hunting down their targets using lists. Their “cleansing operations” have included the execution of dozens of Ukrainian priests , the banning of the Ukrainian language and the torture of journalists and writers , as both news reports and reports by international human rights groups have established.

There is no reason to think Russian forces won’t do all of these same things throughout Ukraine, if given a chance to occupy it.

This is not the first time Russia has tried to exterminate the national identity of a prostrate country. In their infamous pact of August 1939, which set the stage for World War II, the Soviet Union aligned with Nazi Germany, and the two agreed to invade and divide Poland. While occupying the eastern half of Poland, the Soviet secret police , on Stalin’s orders, rounded up some 22,000 Polish Army officers, political leaders, police and border guards, professionals, and intellectuals and shot them — most notoriously in the Katyn Forest .

That is why the collapse of the diesel deal matters. Had the tankers offloaded Russian diesel in American ports, and American dollars started flowing to Russia, the psychological, political, and practical effects would have been devastating to Ukraine and its supporters. The war still hangs in the balance, but the failure of Trump and Putin to break the sanctions regime is a victory for Ukraine in its gallant fight for survival.

Gregory J. Wallance , a writer and former federal prosecutor , is the author of, most recently, “Into Siberia: George Kennan’s Epic Journey Through the Brutal, Frozen Heart of Russia . ”
